reasoning: The core problem -- how much ASR measurements depend on the judge model and how well judges agree on a fixed transcript set -- is heavily studied. "LLM-Safety Evaluations Lack Robustness" (arXiv:2503.02574) shows judge/scoring choices make jailbreak results "vary wildly" and centers StrongREJECT; the NeurIPS 2025 paper "Comparison requires valid measurement" (arXiv:2601.18076) formalizes when ASRs are comparable across judges and documents that judges don't perform equally across attack methods. Multiple works directly compare StrongREJECT vs HarmBench vs JailbreakBench judges, report inter-judge agreement (Krippendorff's alpha, Fleiss/Cohen kappa, pairwise agreement) on shared transcripts, and show judge choice flips the ranking of models/defenses/attacks -- which is exactly the proposal's methodology and "freeze transcripts, swap judge" twist. The only thin remaining gap is a dedicated focus exclusively on open judge models replicating the StrongREJECT rubric, but existing comparisons already include open judges (Llama-3-70B, Llama Guard 2/3, Mistral, Qwen3Guard), leaving only a minor incremental contribution.

evidence.title: LLM-Safety Evaluations Lack Robustness
evidence.summary: Shows that decisions about response sampling and how responses are judged for harmfulness cause jailbreak evaluation results to 'vary wildly.' Discusses StrongREJECT, Llama-Guard-3-8B, and HarmBench classifiers as judges and argues directly using LLM-as-a-judge lacks robustness -- directly addressing the proposal's central question of judge-dependent variance.

evidence.title: Comparison requires valid measurement: Rethinking attack success rate comparisons in AI red teaming (NeurIPS 2025)
evidence.summary: Provides measurement-theory grounding for when ASRs can be meaningfully compared, noting judges do not perform equally across systems/methods and that with explicit pass/fail criteria different judges converge while vague criteria cause divergence. Formalizes the exact judge-variance / cross-judge comparability problem the proposal investigates.

evidence.title: A StrongREJECT for Empty Jailbreaks
evidence.summary: Original StrongREJECT paper; its autograder rubric (0-1 score, GPT-4 judge, threshold-based ASR) is the rubric the proposal would replicate. Already reports judge agreement with human labels and compares against HarmBench/JailbreakBench graders.

evidence.title: PandaGuard: Systematic Evaluation of LLM Safety against Jailbreaking Attacks
evidence.summary: Systematically evaluates multiple judges (HarmBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT) over fixed attack transcripts, reports that judges overestimate ASR differently (e.g., Gemma-2 10% true ASR exaggerated to ~40%) and that StrongREJECT is more accurate -- demonstrating the swap-judge-on-fixed-transcripts methodology is already established.

evidence.title: Why Attack Success Rate (ASR) Isn't Comparable Across Jailbreak Papers Without a Shared Threat Model (Promptfoo)
evidence.summary: Industry writeup summarizing that ASR is not portable across judges/threat models, reinforcing that the dependence of ASR on judge choice is well-recognized and documented, including measured discrepancies between StrongREJECT and HarmBench judges that change model/attack rankings.
